finding_key: packages/backend/src/auth/oauth-state.ts::browser oauth `state` is an unauthenticated double-submit cookie with no `__host-` prefix and no server-side binding, so a sibling-subdomain foothold restores login csrf
evidence: Verified against the supplied oauth-state.ts: `createWebOAuthState` mints a bare `randomBytes(32)` secret and `state = 'web.' + sha256(secret)`, `webOAuthStateMatches` re-hashes whatever is in the cookie with no HMAC or server-side record, and `oauthStateCookieOptions()` sets `path:'/auth'` with no `__Host-` prefix and no Domain pin. Cookie possession is therefore the entire proof, and a sibling host under the registrable domain can write `Domain=example.com; Path=/auth`; auth.controller.ts then matches and falls through to `createTokens`/`setAuthCookies`, issuing a session for the account behind the attacker-supplied code — the sameSite=lax cookie is sent on that top-level GET navigation. This is the known unsigned-double-submit weakness rather than a misreading of the code; I rate it minor rather than higher only because it requires an additional foothold (control of or XSS on a sibling host / takeover-able CNAME) beyond the base login-CSRF scenario the change closed.
